title: Interface engineering of earth-abundant Cu/In(OH)3 catalysts towards electrochemical reduction of CO2 favoring CO selectivity
abstract: Interface engineering has been an alternative strategy applied to catalysts, which is desirable for CO2 electrochemical reduction reaction (ECO2RR) to obtain high selectivity for specific products. Herein, we report Cu/In (OH)3 heterogeneous structure catalyst attached on mildly oxidized carbon nanotubes (CNTs) originating from CuO/In(OH)3 via a facile wet hydrolysis precipitation method for ECO2RR. The selectivity of CO can be tuned by slightly adjusting the In/(Cu + In) (YIn) atomic fraction. Typically, high Faradaic efficiency (FE) of CO (89%) with the partial current density of 10.1 mA/cm2 at –1.0 V(versus a reversible hydrogen electrode, RHE) is obtained at YIn = 4.5%, outperforming the most reported Cu-In based catalysts. The strong interaction between Cu and In(OH)3 are responsible to promote FECO. Designing the metal/metal hydroxide electrocatalysts for electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction opens an alternative opportunity for optimizing efficient and selective catalysts for desired products.

Journal of CO2 Utilization 46 (2021) 101470

Interface engineering of earth-abundant Cu/In(OH)3 catalysts towards electrochemical reduction of CO2 favoring CO selectivity
Wenjuan Li a, Yuhua Yang a, Zhe Weng b,*, Shengjuan Huo a,* a Department of Chemistry, Science Colleges, Shanghai University, 99 Shangda Road, Shanghai, 200444, China b School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Tianjin University, Tianjin, 300072, China
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords: Cu/In(OH)3-CNTs CO2 electrochemical reduction reactions Catalyst Selectivity
A B S T R A C T
Interface engineering has been an alternative strategy applied to catalysts, which is desirable for CO2 electrochemical reduction reaction (ECO2RR) to obtain high selectivity for specific products. Herein, we report Cu/In (OH)3 heterogeneous structure catalyst attached on mildly oxidized carbon nanotubes (CNTs) originating from CuO/In(OH)3 via a facile wet hydrolysis precipitation method for ECO2RR. The selectivity of CO can be tuned by slightly adjusting the In/(Cu + In) (YIn) atomic fraction. Typically, high Faradaic efficiency (FE) of CO (89%) with the partial current density of 10.1 mA/cm2 at –1.0 V(versus a reversible hydrogen electrode, RHE) is obtained at YIn = 4.5%, outperforming the most reported Cu-In based catalysts. The strong interaction between Cu and In(OH)3 are responsible to promote FECO. Designing the metal/metal hydroxide electrocatalysts for electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction opens an alternative opportunity for optimizing efficient and selective catalysts for desired products.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Nowadays, reduction of CO2 to useful fuels by using sustainable energy sources is an alternative strategy to reduce planetary warming and energy crisis [1–3]. Recently, electrochemical of CO2 reduction reaction (ECO2RR) has been drawn wide attention due to the mild reaction conditions and controllable reaction parameters [4,5]. Appropriate electrocatalysts can form various reduction products from ECO2RR [6] and a variety of electrocatalysts have been thoroughly explored so far, including metallic In [7], Cu [8],Ag/Cu [9], Sn [10] metal oxides such as CuO [11],In2O3/ZrO2 [12], ZnO [13], metal chalcogenides such as MoS2 [14], TiS2 [15], metal halides [16,17], molecular catalysts [18–22] and some carbon-based materials [23–26] etc. However, the challenges about complicated mechanism, a large overpotential and poor selectivity are still open to be tackled [27].
Specifically, CO is one of the most promising products from the reduction of CO2 due to the ability to be further reduced to value-added chemicals [28–30]. Noble metals such as Au [31–33], Ag [34–36], and Pd [37,38]have been widely reported for ECO2RR to CO with excellent selectivity. However, the high costs limit the industrial scale up to some extent. The cheaper substituted materials are desirable to enhance selectivity of CO from ECO2RR.
Designing multicomponent catalysts seems a good strategy because of synergistic effects assigned to the electronic and geometric effects of the individual materials [39–42].Copper, as a unique metal, is capable to reduce CO2 to value-added products at a wide potential range [43, 44]. Alloying or surface modification has been proposed to improve selectivity [45]. Many second partners such as Au [46,47], Sn [48], Pd [49,50],In [51], Ag [52] and oxides [53–55] have been incorporated into Cu to promote CO2 reductioninto CO. Our group reported SnOx modified Cu with varying components can tune the selectivity into hydrocarbon, CO or formic acid [56]. Nevertheless, multicomponent catalysts with synergistic effects usually suffered from the limited species and difficult regulation method.As cheap multi-compositional Cu/In materials such as alloy [51], heterogeneous compounds [57], or core-shell structure [58]specially grasped the eyeballs of the researchers. Cu-In alloy catalyst reported by Rasul et al. can efficiently reduce CO2 into CO at a moderate potential [51].However, Cu-In alloy with varied compositions favored selectivity of formic acid rather than CO [59,60]. AlthoughCu/In interface by In3+ deposition on Cu(OH)2 nanowires [61]andCuInO2 nanoparticles [62] can selectively catalyze CO2 to CO, the complicated calcination treatment limited the application. Still, the reaction mechanism and product selectivity over multicomponent catalysts are debatable because of different active centers,

preparation methods, compositions, and/or conductivities [51,58,59, 62]. Moreover, all the above-mentioned catalysts had the common shortcoming of lower CO partial current density (jCO) about 1− 3 mA cm− 2[51,62,63]. Therefore, it is desirable to design a facile preparation method to fabricate the catalyst and boost the jCO. As a result, systematically researching the effect of compositions on products selectivity over Cu-In multicomponent catalysts is valuable to classify the influential factors in electrocatalysis.
Herein, we fabricated the series of CuO/In(OH)3 heterogeneous structured catalysts supported on mildly oxidized carbon nanotubes (CNTs) by a facile two-step hydrolysis precipitation method. Characterization data supported that Cu/In(OH)3 active sites during ECO2RR. Product selectivity and optimization can be tuned by changing the amount of indium precursor. Different from hydrocarbons product by pure CuO and formic acid by pure In(OH)3, the CuO/In(OH)3-CNT catalyst (In/(Cu + In) atomic ratio (YIn) = 4.5%) can electrocatalyze CO2 into CO with high selectivity (89%) and higher jCO of 10.1 mA cm− 2 at –1.0 V (versus a reversible hydrogen electrode, vs. RHE), which is among the top positions for Cu-In based or coinage catalysts. Cu/In (OH)3 active sites during ECO2RR can provide an effective catalytic center and participate in CO formation. The high selectivity of CO can be attributed to that the oxyphilic In(OH)3 combining with Cu can promote stabilizing the *COOH by interacting with one of the O atoms in this multiple-proton transfer reaction and inhibiting the *H adsorption to suppress the H2 evolution. This study can provide a certain theoretical basis and technical guidance for the development of a new type of ECO2RR composite catalyst.

sections.heading: 2.1. Material synthesis
sections.text: To sequentially synthesize the series of CuO/In(OH)3–CNTs catalysts, two-step hydrolysis and precipitation method at mild 80℃ were designed (Table S1). Briefly, CuO nanoparticles were grown on mildly oxidized CNTs through the hydrolyzation of Cu(OAc)2⋅2H2O in NaOH ethanol system in the first step. Then In(OH)3 nanoparticles were supported on the as-prepared CuO/CNT surface through the hydrolyzation of InCl3 in NaOH ethanol solution in the second step. YIn was adjusted by the molar ratio of indium chloride and copper acetate. As comparison, pure CuO/CNT or In(OH)3/CNT was fabricated in one single step for use. The detailed recipe for the above mentioned nanoparticles was listed in Table S1. For purpose of evaluating the role of CNTs, the commercial carbon black (CB) was as a support to run a control experiment as comparison (Fig S1).

sections.heading: 2.2. Working electrode preparation
sections.text: A homogeneous ink for the electrochemical measurement was prepared by mixing 4 mg of the catalyst into 360μL of ethanol and 40 μL of 5 wt % Nafion solution, followed by sonication for more than 30 min. The cathode was prepared by loading 50 μL of the catalyst ink onto carbon paper electrode (GDS 090, 30% PTFE) with an area of 0.5 cm2.

sections.heading: 2.3. Electrochemical testing
sections.text:
CO2 electrochemical reduction experiments were carried out in a home-made gas-tight H-type cell, which was separated by the Nafion 115 membrane. Allelectrochemical measurements were performed by employing an electrochemical workstation (Ivium Vertex. One. EIS) using a three-electrode configuration including prepared CuO/In(OH)3 electrode, graphite rod and Ag/AgCl electrode (in saturated KCl electrolyte) as the working electrode, counter electrode, and a reference electrode, respectively. The 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte was purged with CO2 for 30 min before the measurement and pH value for this electrolyte was 6.8. The working electrode compartment was continuously purged
with CO2 at a flow rate of 20 sccm in the reaction process. All of the applied potentials were converted to RHE using E (vs. RHE) = E (vs. Ag/ AgCl) + 0.197 V + 0.0591 V*pH.

sections.heading: 2.4. Product analysis
sections.text: Gaseous products from the cell were injected via an automatic sample loop into a gas chromatograph and analyzed to determine the concentration of gas products every 10 min. The gas chromatograph (Shimadzu GC-2014) was equipped with a molecular sieve 5A column with argon flowing as a carrier gas. Hydrogen concentration was determined by a thermal conductivity detector, and the concentrations of carbon monoxide, methane, and ethylene were determined using a flame ionization detector. We quantified the liquid products such as formic acid by the ion chromatography (Soptop IC1820). The mobile phase was an aqueous solution of KOH (5 mM, flowing at 0.6 mL min− 1). The concentration of formic acid was determined from the calibration curve obtained by a series of standard formate solutions. Typically, 200 μL of the electrolyte in the cathode chamber was diluted 10 times with deionized water in order to eliminate the trailing peak of HCO3-. Faradaic efficiency (FE) can be determined from the amount of the charge passed to produce each product divided by the total charge passed at a specific time or during the overall run.

sections.heading: 2.5. Structural characterizations
sections.text: X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns for electrocatalysts and the used catalysts coated with carbon paper electrodes were collected on Rigaku SmartLab X-ray Diffractometer (Rigaku Corporation, Japan) equipped with Cu-target X-ray tube (λ = 0.154 nm) and operated at 40 mA at 44 kV. The scan range for the powder were measured from 20 to 80◦ and that for the used electrode from 30 to 80◦ in case of the influence of sharp peak of carbon paper at 27◦. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was performed using PHI VersaProbe II X-ray Photoelectron Spectrometer. The XPS spectra were collected using monochromatic 1486.7 eV Al Ka X-ray source on PHI VersaProbe II X-ray Photoelectron Spectrometer with a 0.47 eV system resolution. The energy scale has been calibrated using Cu 2p3/2 (932.67 eV) and Au 4f7/2 (84.00 eV) peaks on a clean copper plate and a clean gold foil. The Binding energies (B. E.) were calculated from reference C 1s core level at 284.6 eV. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometer (EDS) was conducted for the as-prepared and post-reaction samples with a Hitachi SU8230 at 20 keV. The microstructures of the used catalysts were characterized by transmission electronic microscope (TEM), atomic-scale high-resolution TEM (HR-TEM), selected-area electron diffraction (SAED) on a JEM-2100F. X-ray fluorescence (XRF) measurements (Rigaku ZSXPrimus II) were performed for the average elemental composition.

sections.heading: 3.1. Effect ofIn contents on ECO2RR performance and the structure analysis
sections.text:
CuO and In(OH)3 nanoparticles were sequentially grown on CNT through a solution-phase synthesis (Scheme1 and Table S1). Different YIn in the catalysts were in the 0.17− 11 wt% range (Fig. 1a), determined by XRF spectroscopy. The measured YIn matched reasonably well with the designed ratios (Table S2).To evaluate the activity and selectivity of the series of as-prepared catalysts, CO2 electrolysis were carried out at –1.0 V vs. RHE in 0.1 M KHCO3 for an hour (Fig. 1b and Fig. S1). As substrate, CNTs were not active for ECO2RR and mainly showed performance for hydrogen evolution (86% for H2 and 6% for CO). As contrast, the main product for CuO-CNT-#1 (1 in Fig. 1b) were hydrogen and hydrocarbons and the amounts of CO were negligible. Moreover, formic acid was the dominant reduction product with the FE of 77% for
W. Li et al.
Journal of CO2 Utilization 46 (2021) 101470
In(OH)3-CNT-#9 with the inhibited hydrogen evolution (9 in Fig. 1b), in accordance with the previously reported [64]. As observed, FECO increased with the In amount, reaching a maximum (～89%) at the CuO/In(OH)3-CNT-#6 (YIn = 4.5%) catalyst with the high jCO (10.1 mA cm− 2), implying that the incorporation of In into Cu altered the nature of electrocatalyst centers and generated synergistic effect. What was encouraging was that our high value of jCO outperformed most reported Cu-In catalysts [51,62,63], even surpassed Au [65] and Ag [66,67] that have been shown as excellent catalysts for CO production towards ECO2RR. With YIn continuously increased, the catalysts preferred formic acid generation. Tunable product dependent on composition in our result can possibly support the conclusion that in the previous references CuIn alloys with different contents can electrocatalyze different products [38,60].It should be mentioned CNTs played an important role in improving the conductivity and avoiding agglomeration of CuO/In (OH)3 particles. Other support such as commercial CB was tested as a benchmark (Fig. S1) and the far less selectivity for CO were possibly due to poor dispersibility without electrostatic interaction between metal ions and support. Note that CuO/In(OH)3-CNT-#6 typically
electrocatalyzing CO2 into CO has been systematically focused. As comparison, pristine CuO/CNT-#1 and In(OH)3/CNT-#9 served as the counterparts.
SEM images of the series of as-prepared catalysts and typical three catalysts were presented in Fig. S2 and Fig. 2. The results indicated that CuO and In(OH)3 nanoparticles were granular and have been successfully attached to CNTs. With the improved YIn content, SEM images changed greatly in nanoparticle sizes and shapes.
Fig. 3a showed XRD patterns for the three typical catalysts. Two reflections at approximately 35.1 and 38.0◦ were observed in CuO/In (OH)3-CNT-#6, which can be well assigned to the (002) and (111) planes of CuO, respectively. This indicated the formation of crystalline CuO in the CuO/In(OH)3-CNT-#6, corresponding to the standard card (PDF:44− 0706). The characteristic reflection at 22.6◦ in the CuO/In (OH)3-CNT-#6, coming from the (200) plane of In(OH)3, suggesting that the yield crystalline In(OH)3, consistent with the standard card (PDF:76− 1463) [68]. XPS measurements in Cu 2p and In 3d regions were further performed to probe the chemical state and composition on the surface of the catalysts. As shown in Fig. 3b, c, the BEs at 953.8 and
W. Li et al.
Journal of CO2 Utilization 46 (2021) 101470
933.9 eV can be assigned to Cu 2p1/2 and Cu 2p3/2 regions, indicating the existence of CuO [69,70]. In In 3d region, a doublet at 453.0 and 445.4 eV can be assigned to the 3d3/2 and 3d5/2 peaks, agreed well with that of In(OH)3[61].These results were also consistent with the XRD of the catalysts.
To primarily evaluate the activity of catalysts, the linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) of the series of as-prepared as well as the corresponding used catalysts was exhibited in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 (Fig. S3). The overall current density of CuO/In(OH)3-CNT-#6 was between the pristine CuO/CNT and In(OH)3/CNT, which may be caused by
W. Li et al.
Journal of CO2 Utilization 46 (2021) 101470
the species and properties of catalysts. This trend was consistent with the current density obtained in the chronoamperometry mode at –1.0 V vs. RHE in Fig. 1b. Additionally, the current density of the used catalysts was all lower than the corresponding newly-prepared ones, which may be contributed to the reduction or the surface reconstruction under such a negative potential.

sections.heading: 3.2. Effects of applied potential over the catalysts
sections.text: Fig. 4a-c exhibited the ECO2RR activity of typical three samples at different applied potentials. For CuO-CNT-#1 (Fig. 4a), more than 70% H2 was produced at all potentials, and the amounts of CO was significant smaller. The FE for CH4 reached a maximum at –1.1 V vs. RHE. For CuO/ In(OH)3-CNT-#6 (Fig. 4b), both FE and jCO increased with the potential being more negative until –1.0 V vs. RHE, where the maximum values of FE was 89% with a jCO of 10.1 mA/cm2. For In(OH)3-CNT-#9 (Fig. 4c), a maximum FE for formic acid of 86% was achieved at –1.2 V vs. RHE. Stability was also crucial for a catalyst for practical applications. To evaluate the stability of the excellent CuO/In(OH)3-CNT-#6, ECO2RR test in 0.1 M KHCO3 at –1.0 V versus RHE over an extended period time was carried out, as shown in Fig. 4d. The CuO/In(OH)3-CNT-#6 exhibited relatively stable current density and FEs towards CO, with a relatively low decrease following 5 h of continuous ECO2RR.

sections.heading: 3.3. The structures of the catalysts after ECO2RR
sections.text:
Considering that the real active sites of catalysts can be changed under such a negative potential. Therefore, the morphology and composition of CuO-CNT-#1, CuO/In(OH)3-CNT-#6, and In(OH)3-CNT#9 after ECO2RR at –1.0 V vs. RHE were necessary to further characterize. As shown in Fig. 5a, the diffraction peaks in the XRD patterns of the used catalysts were both belong to metallic Cu (with the strong peak Cu (111) at 43.3◦and Cu (200) at 50.5◦). These results suggested that the CuO nanoparticles were reduced to metallic Cu under the ECO2RR. Diffraction peaks in the used In(OH)3-CNT-#9 was confirmed to
crystalline In(OH)3, exclusive of metallic In (Fig. S4), consistent with the previously reported views [57,71]. What surprised us was that the In (OH)3 was not reduced at such a negative measurement potential though the thermodynamic equilibrium potential for the reduction of In(OH)3 is –0.177 V vs. RHE at PH = 6.8 [72]. Additionally, we ran full cyclic voltammetries (CVs) over In(OH)3-CNT-#9 in Ar and CO2–saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 at a scan rate of 20 mV⋅s− 1 to investigate the redox performance of In(OH)3 (Fig. S5). The result showed that the characteristic oxidation peak of In (ca –0.1 V vs. RHE) was not obvious in Ar or CO2, suggesting that the existence of a strong kinetic impairment for the reduction of In(OH)3 can keep In(OH)3 redox-inactive. This may be caused by the large band gap of In(OH)3[73]. Its electrochemical behavior was largely different from that of In2O3, agreed well with the previous reports [57,71]. On the other hand, it was worth noticing that the half-peak width of the CuO/In(OH)3-CNT-#6 tended to narrow during CO2 electrochemical reduction, which may be due to the surface reconstruction. Furthermore, higher 2θ reflection were observed for the Cu and In(OH)3 in the used CuO/In(OH)3-CNT-#6 compared to their pristine counterparts, possibly be caused by the interactions of Cu and In (OH)3. Fig. 5b, c exhibited the XPS spectra of Cu 2p and In 3d for the used catalysts. The Cu 2p peaks of the CuO-CNT-#1 at BEs of 932.8 and 952.8 eV, indicating that reduced Cu were on the surface of catalysts after ECO2RR. The peaks at 444.8 and 452.4 eV, assigned as In 3d5/2 and In 3d3/2 of CuO/In(OH)3-CNT-#6, proved the existence of In(OH)3[71]. An apparent negative shift of Cu 2p and In 3d BEs in CuO/In (OH)3-CNT-#6 relative to CuO-CNT-#1 and In(OH)3-CNT-#9 can be identified, again revealed the interaction between Cu and In(OH)3 to some extent. Specifically, the tafel slope, which can reflect the kinetics for CO formation [74] was 125.8 mV dec-1 for Cu/In(OH)3-CNT-#6, significantly different from 199.2 and 220.1 mV dec-1 for Cu-CNT-#1 and In(OH)3-CNT-#9, respectively (Fig. 5d). This suggested that the formation of *COOH intermediate on the surface of the catalysts was likely the rate-determining step and addition of Cu displayed faster reaction kinetics than In(OH)3-CNT-#9. Therefore, the corollary probably was that that Cu and In(OH)3 anchored on CNTs played a role as an
W. Li et al.
Journal of CO2 Utilization 46 (2021) 101470
active center during the ECO2RR. SEM and TEM images presented the morphology of the catalysts after
ECO2RR in Fig. 6. As observed, SEM images of Cu-CNT-#1, Cu/In(OH)3CNT-#6 and In(OH)3-CNT-#9 (Fig. 6a-c) were greatly different from those before reaction which possibly be caused by the surface reconstruction in ECO2RR process from surface dissolution and electrocrystallization, and dense nanoparticles gradually accumulated on the CNTs surface for the used catalysts. As illustrated in Fig. 6d-g, TEM was explored to further observe the size of the used CuO/In(OH)3-CNT-#6. The average size was about 2− 5 nm, smaller than that of as-prepared catalyst. HR-TEM analysis (Fig. 6e) presented typical diffraction contrast images which demonstrated the crystalline characteristics of the nano-particles. The crystal fringes with distances of 0.208, 0.398 nm represented Cu (111) and In(OH)3 (200), were in line with the XRD results. The lattice striations of Cu and In(OH)3 were very close together, indicating again the strong interaction between Cu and In(OH)3. The SAED pattern of the used CuO/In(OH)3-CNT-#6 (Fig. 6f) showed polycrystalline Cu and polycrystalline In(OH)3. The clear diffraction rings at 2.5 nm− 1 was from the (200) reflection of In(OH)3 and the diffraction rings at 4.8 nm− 1 was from the (111) reflection of Cu, agreed with the lattice fringes in the HR-TEM image and the previously reported [61]. The weak diffraction rings at 3.5 nm− 1 was from the (220) reflection of In(OH)3. These results further confirmed In(OH)3 and Cu may be the active sites during ECO2RR. HAADF-TEM and the responding EDS elemental maps (Fig. 6g) demonstrated that Cu and In(OH)3 nanoparticles grown in close contact on the surface of CNTs after ECO2RR.

sections.heading: 3.4. The possible contribution in boosting the catalytic properties
sections.text:
The electrochemical reduction mechanism is often an open topic of great concern and has been discussed in previous studies [28,75–77].A common-considered conclusion is that either the *COOH intermediate or *OCOH intermediate on transition metal catalysts is involved in CO2RR [78–81].
*(catalyst) + CO2 + H+ + e− →*COOH (1)
*(catalyst) + CO2 + H+ + e− →*OCHO (2)
The reduction of CO2 to CO is reported to go through the *COOH intermediate, the formation of which follows one of the two pathways: (A) single-step proton-coupled electron transfer or (B) first single electron transfer to form *COO− , and then protonation produces *COOH [82]. Therefore, higher activity for CO production requires the formation of a more stable *COOH on the electrocatalyst surface to promote the CO formation [82]. Electronic and geometric effects can be taken into account for the underlying cause. On one hand, due to the electronic structure alignment at the junction, electron transfer from the hydroxide semiconductor to metal may be favorable [56]. The resulted increase in electron density on the Cu site may strengthen the binding of *COOH (CO2 is a Lewis acid) but weaken the binding of *CO (CO is a Lewis base) and thus favors CO2 reduction to CO [56]. This was similar to the effect on previously reported Ag/ In(OH)3[57] and Cu/SnOx [56]. On the other hand, In(OH)3 has good affinity to oxygen [57,62], which can provide a dual site with adjacent Cu site to promote stabilizing the *COOH by interacting with one of the O atoms in this multiple-proton transfer reaction.This geometric synergistic effect contributes to a more stable *COOH intermediate which has the observed selectivity for CO. Besides, the effect of *H binding was as well significant on the selectivity of products in ECO2RR. By DFT calculation, Züttel et al. concluded that higher free energy was required for *H adsorption on Cu-In than mono-component Cu and pointed that the interface can better stabilize *COOH to generate CO and inhibit H2 evolution [61]. Wang et al. also pointed that the introduction of In doped Cu@Cu2O can change *H adsorption and inhibit H2 evolution [58]. Taken together, the formation of more stable *COOH by geometric and electron synergistic effects as well as the weakly binding of *H over Cu/In(OH)3 contributed to the enhanced selectivity for CO and suppressed H2 evolution [51,58, 61,63].
W. Li et al.
Journal of CO2 Utilization 46 (2021) 101470

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
In summary, we have fabricated the series of CuO/In(OH)3-CNT by a facile hydrolysis method of metallic salt in ethanol solution and revealed that structure-activity relationship for ECO2RR. CuO/In(OH)3-CNT was reduced to Cu/In(OH)3 as the active site during CO2 electroreduction, which showed comparatively excellent performance for CO2 reduction. The activity and selectivity can be tuned by varying the YIn different from their pristine counterpart. Higher CO reduction current density on the as-prepared Cu/In(OH)3-CNT electrocatalyst was identified, outperforming most of the reported Cu-In based catalysts. The surface reconstruction during CO2 electroreduction between In(OH)3 and CuO would help elucidate the identity of the active sites and the exact nature of the synergistic eff ;ect. The low-cost, earth-abundant catalysts point out the new catalyst application perspective as well. The structural insights from this study also provide valuable guidelines for the development of excellent new-type catalysts for energy conversion.
